title: ISRO launches NVS-03 on GSLV-F18 in bid to restore India's NavIC navigation system
dek: The rocket lifted off from Sriharikota at 11:51 pm on Friday. The real test comes in the next few days, when the satellite must raise its own orbit, the step at which its predecessor failed.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) launched the navigation satellite NVS-03 on its GSLV-F18 rocket from Sriharikota at 11:51 pm IST on Friday, October 30, in a mission meant to bring India's own satellite navigation system, NavIC, back to the minimum strength it needs to work on its own.

The rocket lifted off from the Second Launch Pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, ISRO said in a post on X. The Deccan Chronicle reported shortly after midnight that the rocket had injected the satellite of about 2,250 kg into its planned geosynchronous transfer orbit. The harder part of the mission now begins: in 2025 the previous satellite in the series, NVS-02, reached the same kind of orbit and then could not be moved any further.

## What happened

The GSLV-F18 was the 20th flight of the Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle, according to ISRO and All India Radio. The rocket, about 50 metres tall and weighing about 420 tonnes at lift-off according to The Week, uses a solid core booster with four liquid-fuelled strap-on motors, a liquid second stage and an Indian-built cryogenic upper stage that burns liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen.

According to figures published before the launch by The Tribune and The Week, the cryogenic stage was to release NVS-03 into a long oval orbit about 170 km above Earth at its lowest point and 37,023 km at its highest. From there the satellite must fire its own engine several times over the coming days to round off that orbit and climb to its working position about 36,000 km up, where it will appear to hang over the Indian region.

At the time of writing, The Declaration had not seen a detailed ISRO statement on the satellite's separation, its achieved orbit or its health. This report will be updated when ISRO confirms them.

NVS-03 carries an Indian-built atomic clock alongside clocks bought from abroad, All India Radio reported. Accurate timekeeping is the heart of any satellite navigation system: receivers on the ground work out their position by measuring how long signals take to arrive from several satellites. The satellite also adds a civilian L1 signal, the band used by GPS and most consumer phones, to NavIC's existing L5 and S-band signals, which should make it easier for ordinary devices to use NavIC. The system is designed to cover India and an area up to about 1,500 km beyond its borders.

## Background

NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation), earlier called IRNSS, is India's regional alternative to the American GPS. It was built so that India would not have to depend on a foreign system for positioning and timing, which are used by everything from aircraft and ships to telecom networks, power grids and banking.

The system has been short of working satellites for some time. In a reply in Parliament on July 29, 2026, the government said only three satellites, IRNSS-1B, IRNSS-1I and NVS-01, were providing positioning, navigation and timing services, The Week reported. At least four are needed for a receiver to fix its position independently, and the full constellation is designed for seven.

The second-generation NVS series was meant to fix that. NVS-01 was launched in May 2023. NVS-02 followed in January 2025 on GSLV-F15, as ISRO's 100th launch from Sriharikota, and reached its transfer orbit. But the valves that should have let fuel and oxidiser flow to its main engine never opened, so the satellite could not be raised to its working orbit.

The Week, citing the findings of ISRO's review, reported that the fault was traced to a contact that had come loose in a connector on the oxidiser line. The valves involved are pyro valves, one-time switches opened by a small explosive charge, and the break cut off both the main and the backup signal at once. A failure analysis committee was headed by former ISRO chairman A S Kiran Kumar, according to The Tribune.

Union Minister Jitendra Singh, who oversees the space department, has said the problems have been corrected and that the fix was tested on the communication satellite CMS-03, launched by an LVM3 rocket on November 2, 2025, The Week reported. Some reports before the launch said ISRO might open the pyro valves on the ground before lift-off this time; ISRO had not confirmed this.

## What they are saying

All India Radio said before the launch that a successful deployment would restore NavIC's basic operational requirement of four satellites.

Space analyst Girish Linganna told The Week that "the real test for NVS-03 begins where its sibling fell silent", a reference to the orbit-raising stage at which NVS-02 failed.

Ravi Gupta, a former scientist with the Defence Research and Development Organisation, told reporters before the launch that NavIC would become fully operational once the satellite was in place, according to India.com and Republic.

## What happens next

ISRO's ground stations will now command a series of engine firings to lift NVS-03 to its final orbit. If those burns work, the satellite will go through in-orbit tests of its clocks and signals before it can be commissioned into service, a process that usually takes weeks.

Even then, NavIC will have only the bare minimum of four working navigation satellites. NVS-04 and NVS-05 are in their final stages of preparation, according to The Week, and one more satellite will be needed after them to complete the planned seven.

## Key numbers

- Lift-off: 11:51 pm IST, October 30, 2026
- Rocket: GSLV-F18, the 20th GSLV flight
- Satellite mass: about 2,250 kg (The Week gives 2,232 kg)
- Planned transfer orbit: about 170 km x 37,023 km
- NavIC satellites providing navigation before this launch: 3 (government reply, July 2026)
- Minimum needed for independent positioning: 4; full design: 7
